explanation: Dorsal root ganglia contain nerve cells of VARIABLE size (not same size) - large neurons for proprioception, medium for touch, small for pain. Lateral division of dorsal root carries pain and temperature; medial division carries proprioception and fine touch. Thick myelinated fibers carry proprioceptive information.
keyConcept: DRG neurons: variable sizes (large=proprioception, small=pain); lateral = pain/temp; medial = touch/proprioception.

explanation: DRG neurons are of variable size (pseudounipolar neurons with different diameters). The ganglion is located on the dorsal root OUTSIDE the CNS (not inside), surrounded by a connective tissue capsule. It is not located at viscera.
keyConcept: DRG: pseudounipolar neurons of variable size, encapsulated, located on dorsal root outside CNS.

explanation: DRG cells are pseudounipolar with multiple processes (one peripheral, one central). They have eccentric nuclei, are associated with both myelinated and unmyelinated fibers, and are surrounded by satellite glial cells (not Schwann cells around the cell body itself).
keyConcept: DRG cells: pseudounipolar, multiple processes, eccentric nucleus, satellite cells, myelinated + unmyelinated fibers.

explanation: CNS is NOT rich in connective tissue - it is poor in CT, derived mainly from neuroectoderm. It IS soft, jelly-like (due to high water content), and has both grey matter (cell bodies) and white matter (myelinated fibers).
keyConcept: CNS: poor in CT, soft/jelly-like (high water), has grey (neurons) and white (myelinated) matter.

explanation: Dura mater is a fibrous, avascular layer (contains few blood vessels). It forms the outermost meninx. Arachnoid has trabeculae; pia is vascular; arachnoid barrier layer is cellular. Dura's toughness comes from collagen fibers.
keyConcept: Dura mater: tough outer meninx, fibrous, relatively avascular; attached to periosteum of skull/vertebrae.

explanation: Pia mater is highly vascular (contains blood vessels that penetrate to supply superficial brain tissue). It is the innermost meninx, in direct contact with brain. Arachnoid contains spaces (subarachnoid) for CSF, not pia. Dura contains venous sinuses.
keyConcept: Pia mater: highly vascular, innermost meninx, follows brain contours closely.

explanation: Protoplasmic astrocytes (in grey matter) have numerous short branching processes. Fibrous astrocytes (in white matter) have few long unbranched processes. Both types express GFAP and have foot processes on blood vessels.
keyConcept: Protoplasmic astrocytes: grey matter, numerous short processes. Fibrous astrocytes: white matter, few long processes.

explanation: Tanycytes are specialized ependymal cells that line the third ventricle and other ventricular surfaces, particularly in the hypothalamus. They have long basal processes that extend to blood vessels and are involved in neuroendocrine regulation.
keyConcept: Tanycytes: specialized ependymal cells lining 3rd ventricle, transport molecules between brain and CSF.

explanation: Ependymal cells have cilia on their apical surface that help circulate CSF. They also have microvilli but cilia are the distinguishing feature. The ciliary movement helps propel CSF through the ventricles.
keyConcept: Ependymal cells: ciliated simple columnar epithelium lining ventricles; cilia circulate CSF.

explanation: The cerebral aqueduct connects the 3rd and 4th ventricles but has NO choroid plexus - it is just a narrow channel through the midbrain. Choroid plexus is present in lateral ventricles, 3rd ventricle, and 4th ventricle.
keyConcept: Choroid plexus: lateral, 3rd, and 4th ventricles. NOT in cerebral aqueduct (midbrain).

explanation: The central canal is lined by simple columnar to cuboidal epithelium that is partially ciliated. This ependymal lining continues throughout the ventricular system. The cilia help circulate CSF within the canal.
keyConcept: Central canal: lined by partially ciliated simple columnar-cuboidal epithelium (ependymal cells).

explanation: Oligodendrocytes are derived from neuroectoderm (neural tube/glial precursors), same as neurons and astrocytes. Microglia are derived from mesoderm (monocyte-macrophage lineage), making them the only non-ectodermal glial cells in the CNS.
keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes: neuroectoderm. Microglia: mesoderm (monocyte origin). Astrocytes: neuroectoderm.

explanation: Oligodendrocytes form myelin sheaths in the CNS (one oligodendrocyte can myelinate multiple axons). Schwann cells do this in the PNS. Astrocytes provide support; satellite cells support neurons in ganglia; ependymal cells line ventricles.
keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes: CNS myelin (multiple axons). Schwann cells: PNS myelin (one axon each).

explanation: Microglia are the resident macrophages of the CNS, derived from mesoderm. They become activated in injury and disease to phagocytose debris. Astrocytes and oligodendrocytes are not phagocytic under normal conditions.
keyConcept: Microglia: CNS macrophages (phagocytic), mesodermal origin, activated in injury/disease.

explanation: In CNS injury, astrocytes proliferate (gliosis) to form glial scars, and microglia activate to phagocytose debris. This reactive gliosis is a hallmark of CNS injury response. Oligodendrocytes and ependymal cells do not become abundant.
keyConcept: CNS injury response: astrocyte proliferation (gliosis) + microglia activation (phagocytosis).

explanation: Astrocytes (specifically their foot processes) are key components of the blood-brain barrier, forming a protective layer around capillaries. They induce endothelial cells to form tight junctions. Ependymal cells form blood-CSF barrier, not BBB.
keyConcept: Blood-brain barrier: astrocyte foot processes + tight junction endothelial cells; excludes many substances.

explanation: Grey matter appears grey because it contains nerve cell bodies (unmyelinated or lightly myelinated). White matter appears white due to myelin on axons. The distribution of myelin determines the distribution of grey and white matter.
keyConcept: Grey matter: neuron cell bodies. White matter: myelinated axons. Myelin determines white/grey distribution.

explanation: The blood-CSF barrier is formed by the choroid plexus epithelium (border cells of arachnoid matter - actually choroid plexus cells), not ependymal cells. Ependymal cells line ventricles. The barrier consists of fenestrated capillaries + choroid plexus epithelium with tight junctions.
keyConcept: Blood-CSF barrier: choroid plexus epithelium + fenestrated capillaries + tight junctions.

explanation: Grey matter contains neuron cell bodies, glial cells, and unmyelinated nerve fibers. Myelinated nerve fibers are characteristic of WHITE matter, not grey matter. This is why grey matter appears grey (neuron cell bodies) and white matter appears white (myelin).
keyConcept: Grey matter: cell bodies, dendrites, unmyelinated fibers. White matter: myelinated axons.

explanation: Martinotti cells have axons directed UPWARDS (toward the cortical surface). Their dendrites extend laterally, cell bodies are multipolar (not rounded), and they use various neurotransmitters. They are inhibitory interneurons in the cortex.
keyConcept: Martinotti cells: cortical interneurons with ascending axons; deliver inhibitory signals to superficial layers.

explanation: Inner pyramidal cells (also called Betz cells when giant) are found in layer V of the motor cortex, not in layers I-IV. Layer V is the internal pyramidal layer. The options I-IV are incorrect - inner pyramidal refers to layer V.
keyConcept: Layer V (internal pyramidal): Betz cells, corticospinal neurons. Layer IV: thalamocortical input.

explanation: Giant cells of Betz are found in the INNER PYRAMIDAL layer (layer V) of the motor cortex. These are the largest neurons in the CNS and give rise to corticospinal tract fibers. They are characteristic of the primary motor area.
keyConcept: Betz cells: giant pyramidal neurons in layer V of motor cortex; corticospinal tract origin.

explanation: Cerebral cortex has both laminar (6 layers) and columnar (functional minicolumns) organization. It has a folded surface (gyri and sulci), varying thickness, different neuron shapes in different layers, and shows plasticity.
keyConcept: Cerebral cortex: 6 layers, columnar organization, folded surface, varying thickness, high plasticity.

explanation: Cells of Cajal (horizontal cells) are found in the MOLECULAR layer of the CEREBRAL cortex. They have horizontal axons that run parallel to the surface. In cerebellum, this layer contains Purkinje cells, not Cajal cells.
keyConcept: Cajal cells: horizontal cells in molecular layer of cerebral cortex; horizontal axon orientation.

explanation: Purkinje layer is a layer of the CEREBELLAR cortex, not cerebral cortex. The cerebral cortex layers are: molecular (I), external granular (II), external pyramidal (III), internal granular (IV), internal pyramidal (V), multiform (VI).
keyConcept: Cerebral cortex 6 layers: I molecular, II external granular, III external pyramidal, IV internal granular, V internal pyramidal, VI multiform. Cerebellar cortex: molecular, Purkinje, granular.

explanation: Pia mater is formed of modified fibroblasts (mesenchymal cells) arranged in a thin connective tissue layer. It is not epithelial (not squamous or columnar). The outer surface faces the subarachnoid space, and the inner surface is in contact with brain.
keyConcept: Pia mater: modified fibroblasts (mesenchymal CT), highly vascular, innermost meninx.

explanation: The inner surface of dura mater (which faces the arachnoid) is lined by simple squamous epithelium (mesothelium). The outer surface is attached to periosteum. This creates the dural sinus spaces between the two layers.
keyConcept: Dura mater: outer surface = periosteum; inner surface = simple squamous mesothelium facing arachnoid.

explanation: The brain-CSF barrier is formed by ependymal cells connected by tight junctions, basement membrane, and astrocyte foot processes. Fenestrated endothelial cells are NOT part of this barrier - the brain capillary endothelium has tight junctions forming the blood-brain barrier.
keyConcept: Brain-CSF barrier: ependymal tight junctions + basement membrane + astrocyte foot processes.

explanation: Foot processes of astrocytes are part of the BLOOD-BRAIN barrier, not the blood-CSF barrier. The blood-CSF barrier consists of fenestrated capillaries, basement membrane, and choroid plexus epithelium (connected by tight junctions).
keyConcept: Blood-CSF barrier: fenestrated capillaries + choroid epithelium with tight junctions. Blood-brain barrier: tight junction endothelium + astrocyte foot processes.

explanation: Tight junctions between ependymal cells form the brain-CSF barrier, limiting passage between ventricles and brain parenchyma. The blood-brain barrier involves astrocyte foot processes and tight junction endothelial cells.
keyConcept: Ependymal tight junctions = brain-CSF barrier. Astrocyte foot processes + endothelial tight junctions = blood-brain barrier.

explanation: GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein) is an intermediate filament protein specific to astrocytes. It is used as a marker to identify astrocytes in histology and neuropathology. Oligodendrocytes, microglia, and ependymal cells do not contain GFAP.
keyConcept: GFAP: astrocyte marker (intermediate filament). Used to identify astrocytes in CNS.

explanation: Cerebellar islands (islands of granular cells) contain rosettes of mossy fiber terminals surrounded by dendrites of granule cells. Mossy fibers synapse with granule cell dendrites in these glomeruli.
keyConcept: Cerebellar glomeruli: mossy fiber rosettes + granule cell dendrites; input from spinal cord/brainstem.

explanation: Cerebellar glomeruli contain rosettes of mossy fibers, dendrites of granule cells, and axons of Golgi cells (inhibitory). They do NOT contain dendrites of basket cells - those are involved in different synapses on Purkinje cell bodies.
keyConcept: Cerebellar glomerulus: mossy fiber rosette + granule cell dendrites + Golgi cell axons. Basket cells synapse on Purkinje soma.

explanation: Purkinje cells are the SOLE OUTPUT of the cerebellar cortex - their axons are the only fibers leaving the cortex to deeper nuclei. These axons are inhibitory (GABAergic). Golgi, basket, and granule cells are all interneurons.
keyConcept: Purkinje cells: only efferent of cerebellar cortex; GABAergic; projects to deep nuclei and vestibular nuclei.

explanation: The cerebellar cortex is NOT uniform - different regions have different afferent inputs (vestibular, spinocerebellar, corticocerebellar). It has 3 layers (molecular, Purkinje, granular), not 6. It does show sulci (folia).
keyConcept: Cerebellar cortex: 3 layers (molecular, Purkinje, granular), folia/sulci, non-uniform structure.
